brief.situation: 09:00 on a medical-surgical unit. You have five patients, with Sam (LPN) and Jo (nursing assistant).
handover: Room 12: an admission arriving now from the emergency department (pneumonia).
Room 14, Mr. Lane, 70: admitted yesterday for back pain; takes ibuprofen at home; 06:00 vital signs normal.
Room 15, Ms. Ruiz: discharge at 11:00 on a new insulin pen. Rooms 16 and 17: stable, scheduled oral medicines.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Plan who does what, give directions, then supervise: reports come back to you as the round goes on.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. The case ends at 10:30, then a debrief scores what you did.

source.note: FLAG: authored. Mr. Lane's bleeding ulcer worsens about 0.01 a minute (0 = stable, 1 = collapse) until a nurse evaluates him and the provider acts. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
FLAG: authored. He faints on the way to the bathroom: the harm outcome. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The assistant's 09:00 vital signs round reaches Mr. Lane about 15 minutes in.
With vague directions the assistant finishes the round and mentions the low reading at the 09:45 huddle. FLAG.
The provider calls back about 5 minutes after an SBAR and gives orders.

cues.question: Which tasks did you keep, which did you delegate and to whom, and what makes a delegation safe?

parts.label: Who does what
parts.criteria: Keeps the admission assessment and the insulin teaching (assessment, teaching and evaluation are nursing judgment); gives the stable patients' scheduled oral medicines to the LPN; gives vital signs to the assistant.
parts.modelAnswer: I keep the admission assessment and Ms. Ruiz's insulin teaching. Sam gives the scheduled oral medicines to the stable patients. Jo does the vital signs round.

parts.label: Making it safe
parts.criteria: Names the five rights; gives specific directions with report-back limits; evaluates any abnormal report personally and escalates; follows up with the team because accountability stays with the RN.
parts.modelAnswer: The five rights: right task, circumstance, person, directions and supervision. Jo gets specific limits to report at once (SBP under 100, heart rate over 110, dizziness). If she reports one, I assess the patient myself, not hand it to Sam, and I escalate; and I check back with both, because I remain accountable.

scoring.modelReasoning: Keep what needs nursing judgment: the admission assessment and the insulin teaching. Give the stable patients' scheduled oral medicines to the LPN and the vital signs round to the assistant, with specific directions: by when, and exactly what to report at once (SBP under 100, heart rate over 110, dizziness). When the assistant reports Mr. Lane's low pressure and wooziness, assess him yourself: black stool on ibuprofen with a low pressure is a possible upper GI bleed, so give the provider an SBAR. Then check back with the team: supervision and evaluation are the fifth right, and the RN remains accountable.

dQ.ask: While Jo does the round: which of the five rights is 'tell me at once if the systolic is under 100'?
dQ.explain: Clear directions say what to do, by when, and exactly what to report. The RN still evaluates what comes back: assessment and evaluation are not delegated.
